https://www.budapesttimes.hu/diplomacy/m.text: The Budapest Times Magyar demands Europe pay its share on borders — or else A strong Europe and a strong European Union cannot exist without a strong Central Europe, and a strong Central Europe cannot exist without the Visegrád Four (V4) — said Péter Magyar, Prime Minister, at the V4 and Ireland heads of government meeting in Bratislava on Thursday. The Prime Minister elaborated that V4 cooperation cannot exist without a strong Poland, Czech Republic, Slovakia and Hungary either, which is why it is welcome that the Visegrád countries have resolved to consult even more intensively and more frequently. He stressed that a reinvigorated V4 will be very successful, and that Europe too will benefit from the fact that what the Visegrád countries commit to, they will also follow through on. Péter Magyar welcomed the fact that he and his Visegrád partners spoke about specifics. “The V4 is a very important form of regional cooperation,” he said. Speaking about the specific topics discussed at the meeting, the Prime Minister noted that they talked about “money, energy, and the fight against illegal migration.” The Prime Minister also highlighted the importance of border protection. “We are proud that together we protect Europe’s external borders, our own borders, and we are proud — regardless of what colour governments have done it — that we live in the safest region of Europe,” he said. Péter Magyar stated that it is not acceptable for Hungary to pay one million euros a day to protect Europe’s common borders. He said he did not want to “Brussels-bash,” but argued that it was not right for Hungary to pay one million euros a day to defend Europe’s common borders and Hungary’s own border, “while another prime minister receives 200 million euros from the European Commission, possibly for failing to do his job.” “This is very much not right. This is not a good message,” the prime minister said, also thanking the Czech prime minister for his solidarity on the matter. On the subject of illegal migration, he stressed that the world had changed enormously, and that the position Hungary, Slovakia, the Czech Republic and Poland had stood alone with at the outset was now the majority view. Within the European Union, not 10 but 19–20 member states were saying the same thing — that a consistent, firm response was needed and that border protection must be supported — he added, expressing hope that an agreement on combating illegal migration could be reached at the October European Council meeting. He also expressed hope that the Irish EU presidency would achieve progress on the EU’s seven-year budget. On Hungary’s part, he promised a constructive yet frank and consistent stance, stressing that he could only accept an agreement in which the interests of Hungarian companies and people were fully upheld. In his view, a proposal in which less money was on offer while centralisation increased and ever more conditions were imposed would not be acceptable. On the topic of competitiveness, he stressed that in the EU’s next seven-year budget he wants to see concrete numerical proposals on how much support companies in Central Europe, for example, will receive — whether for the transition away from Russian gas and oil, for the complete phase-out of fossil energy, or for storage capacities. He also spoke about what he sees as a lack of solidarity from Europe. He argued that solidarity began to fade from the European Union — and cohesion policy began to be taken less and less seriously — precisely when Hungary and 9 other countries joined in 2004. He stressed that the peoples of Central Europe are entitled to the same support that countries which joined earlier, such as Ireland, Spain, or Portugal, received. Péter Magyar recalled that last summer Hungary had to build a sill on the Danube to ensure the operation of the Paks nuclear power plant, and he thanked Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico for his country’s assistance in stabilising the water level on the Danube. At the same time, he noted that the European Union had not asked how it could help — and that one or two member states had even reported Hungary over the sill. He stressed that in such a situation, solidarity should be shown. On the subject of fuel prices, he said that several member states have or had price caps on fuels, but everyone has seen that the crisis at the Strait of Hormuz is not going away, and moreover Russia — for the first time in its history — is not exporting but importing diesel in enormous quantities. He indicated that fuel shortages would arise if the various member states maintained their price caps, so they agreed that “this cannot continue.” In response to a question about the EU budget, he stated that the budget must be fair. It cannot be the case that the very funds intended to reduce disparities are being withheld, he said. He explained that although net contributors pay more, supporting less developed member states is also beneficial for net contributors, since if EU countries develop, that is good for the entire European market. He also believed that agriculture must be given attention, as there are enormous problems in the sector — drought has pushed agriculture “to the brink of existence” not only in Hungary but across Europe. In response to another question — concerning the daily one-million-euro fine imposed on Hungary — Péter Magyar said this court ruling stemmed from a regulation that bears no resemblance to how refugee policy in Europe looks today. At the same time, the prospects for an agreement are good, because “it is not a matter of Hungary vetoing or blackmailing or threatening” — rather, the situation in Europe has fundamentally changed, he said. He also touched on the fact that Hungary has not introduced the migration pact and has not begun to implement it, yet regardless of this, thanks to the fence and Hungary’s legislative environment, people smugglers know that Hungary is not the direction to head in. He therefore stressed that it is completely out of the question for Hungary to relax these rules even slightly. https://seenandheard-international.com/2.text: Czech Republic Dvořák Prague International Music Festival 2026 – Debussy, Kučera, Schulhoff, and Ravel: Daniel Matejča (violin), Sakura Toba (cello), Prague Radio Symphony Orchestra / Elias Grandy (conductor). Dvořák Hall, Rudolfinum, Prague, 15.9.2026. (MB) Elias Grandy conducting the Prague Radio Symphony Orchestra © Dvořákova Praha. Debussy – Prélude à l’après-midi d’un faune Jan Kučera – Double Concerto for violin and cello (world premiere) Schulhoff – Symphony No.1, Op.50 Ravel – Boléro Founded at the dawn of the wireless age in 1926 as the twenty-strong Radiojournal Orchestra, the Prague Radio Symphony Orchestra (Symfonický orchestr Českého rozhlasu) will celebrate its centenary throughout the coming season. A little later this month, that season’s opening concert will recreate its opening programme, offering music by Smetana, Beethoven, Dvořak, and Fibich. As a prelude, this concert, part of the Dvořák Prague International Music Festival (Dvořákova Praha), welcomed its new chief conductor and artistic director Elias Grandy and renewed its record in new music, then and now, Czech and otherwise, albeit with somewhat unexpected results. Prélude à l’après-midi d’un faune has often been claimed as the dawn of modern music. It depends, of course, what one means – even the Bible has two creation stories – but Debussy’s softly subversive tone-poem has as good a claim as any—and was not three decades old when Josef/Jožka Charvat, a pupil of Janáček lifted his baton for that first concert. The performance’s mood was felt in its opening flute solo, which lightly yet unmistakeably infected the orchestra, or so it seemed. I mean no disrespect to Grandy when I say it is better not to pay too much attention to the conductor’s workings here, especially one so outwardly demonstrative, but crucially it did not feel over-conducted. At any rate, due languor – that inescapable word here – was elicited, with outstanding playing here and elsewhere from the orchestra, its warmth just the faunish thing, subsequent arabesques suggestive and provocative. Tristan und Isolde was in the air, but it was also a memory — like the faun’s amorous escapades, imaginary or real. Harps told us much, as did crotales. Time was almost up for a magical, deceptively light opening that left one wanting more. The world premiere of Jan Kučerá’s Double Concerto for violin and cello was a more puzzling affair: not only in relative but more-or-less absolute terms the least advanced work in musical language, form, and much else, of the four on offer, though all but a century newer than the latest (Ravel’s Boléro ). Does that matter? Not necessarily, though we are not talking about Webern or Varèse here. What concerned me more was an almost televisual sectionalism to the outward movements, suggesting they might accompany a broadcast we could not see and without which they did not, at least to my ears, make a great deal of sense. The first of three movements opened promisingly enough, with a cello solo as Romantic cry de profundis from Sakura Toba, soon joined in violin-cello duet by the similarly excellent Daniel Matejča, both soloists collaborating well in what soon became rather jolly. It was not exactly ‘like’ Prokofiev, but there was a good deal of ‘side-slipping’ and, at its best a welcome sense of theatricality. Continuing in neo-Romantic vein, it was for the most part well-fashioned, but the agglomerative sense, without much in the way of transition, of section after section here and in the finale soon began to pall. The central slow movement, a lullaby, cohered better, its opening suggesting something darker, a little more adventurous, although unabashedly tonal: more in texture, then, than in harmony. Its melodic thread had just enough elements of unpredictability to hold one’s attention. A fiddling rondo theme announced the third movement, thereafter shared with cello, provoking a more lyrical response: very much what one might have expected, prior to a puzzling, once again ‘Russian’ waltz interlude and double cadenza. The piece received an enthusiastic reception, however nonplussed I may have been. Erwin Schulhoff’s 1925 First Symphony packed, by contrast, quite a punch: perhaps not entirely successful, but largely so and always intriguing. This was new music to me in the most straightforward sense. Its first movement was haunted by pentatonicism and by Stravinsky — but perhaps not the Stravinsky one might have expected, that of Le Rossignol . Schulhoff here was already assured enough to engage in Stravinskian theft from the master himself, thereafter to proceed along a different, Neue Sachlichkeit path. Rhythm and harmonic rhythm evinced theatricality, but as a view from the concert hall. Was that Debussy’s Prélude in the air of the second of three movements, an Andante con moto ? If not, programming and performance cunningly suggested it, alongside darker, Berg-like material in which the Prague strings truly excelled. This is how to do allusion — and illusion. Grandy shaped its progress well without undue moulding, likewise in a finale that intensified many of these tendencies in an assured, committed performance. Boléro did its thing, resonating with invigorating splendour and clarity in the main hall of the Rudolfinum. Solo spots brought, in context, reminiscence of other works: flute, naturally, with Debussy and bassoon with Schulhoff. But Ravel’s piece was only ever itself in a reading that built in carefully constructed colour. Each of the soloists clearly enjoyed their moment, none more so than the trombonist. My sole cavil was the way Grandy pulled around, even mauled, the close. Yes, there must be, can hardly not be, a wrench, but that comes of itself. It was a pity, but not enough to undo an otherwise fine performance and concert. https://www.dw.com/en/new-eu-plan-for-ar.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OTZL Greenland's melting ice sheet is a climate risk which is contributing to global sea level rise [FILE: May 5, 2021] Image: Ulrik Pedersen/NurPhoto/picture alliance Advertisement The EU on Tuesday presented a new Arctic Strategy that outlines the bloc's priorities in the key region amid challenges such as security threats, climate change and mining. Russia is building up its military power in the Arctic, and US President Donald Trump has threatened Greenland , saying the Danish territory is needed for American security interests but later signed a deal with Denmark over US military access to the territory . China is also investing in the region and has shipping ambitions there. The northern parts of Finland and Sweden, along with Greenland are located within the Arctic, meaning part of the region is in the European neighborhood. Iceland and Norway, two other Arctic states, are also involved in the European single market. 'Tectonic plates of geopolitics' colliding in Arctic "The Arctic is one place where the tectonic plates of geopolitics are colliding," European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said. "When we see that sovereignty, territorial integrity and the rules that have underpinned security in the region can no longer be taken for granted, we have to act and change our strategic posture," she added. EU High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy Kaja Kallas said Russia "has reopened Soviet-era bases and is testing new weapons" in the Arctic. "Drone incursions, GPS jamming and the sabotage of undersea cables undermine Arctic security," Kallas continued. Russia's shadow fleet, which is an attempt to circumvent Western sanctions , is active in the Arctic. On Arctic security, the EU plans to develop a maritime security hub in the region "to facilitate information sharing form seabed to space." The bloc also intends to expand European icebreaker capacity and extend its satellite surveillance program in the region. Russia's Arctic buildup is Iceland's security headache To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video However, the EU does not intend to compete with NATO in the region, EU Commissioner for International Partnerships Jozef Sikela told DW. Twenty-three EU countries are members of NATO. "NATO will remain basically the center of defense and the center of deterrence, but NATO doesn't have a budget, the member state has," Sikela said. "This is first about the proper focus and the proper use of resources of the NATO member states and about better coordination." EU Arctic strategy highlights security and raw materials To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video EU to boost climate research as Arctic faces ice melting crisis In regard to the climate, the Arctic is warming about four times faster than the global average. The melting of ice and glaciers in the Arctic pose risks to Europe such as prolonged heatwaves, drought and flooding. Sikela said, "Collaboration among the Arctic is very difficult," adding, "We're not getting information about the permafrost from the biggest part of the Arctic territory." Sikela accused Russia of "unprecedented" actions in the Arctic and said the "catastrophic level of drilling and opening new mines" in the region is contributing to its rapid warming. The Arctic is rich in critical minerals and rare earth elements such as nickel. As part of the EU Arctic Strategy, the bloc intends "to strengthen climate research, observation and monitoring" and launch flagship projects utilizing AI to "anticipate extreme weather and cascading disasters such as coastal flooding." Norway, which is not an EU member state, is home to Western Europe's largest LNG plant near the city of Hammerfest [FILE: March 14, 2024] Image: Lisi Niesner/REUTERS Although Russia and other non-EU countries such as Norway drill in the Arctic, the EU does not want to expand new drilling in the region. European Commissioner for Energy and Housing Dan Jorgensen said the EU's view "on drilling in the Arctic remains the same and it's very clear: oil, coal and gas must stay in the ground." Greenland submarine cable route project bypasses US Regarding economic interests in the Arctic, the bloc may take further steps to bypass the US. The strategy calls for "resilient submarine cable connectivity linking Greenland directly to Europe, with potential future extensions towards Canada and Japan." The EU also outlined new plans regarding the residents of the Arctic region. The bloc wants to strengthen dialogue with Indigenous people along with expanding Erasmus+ opportunities for Arctic youth.
